scenarios.title: The concert ticket drop
scenarios.scenario:
A ticketing site sells 50,000 seats for a stadium concert. Sales open at 10:00:00 and about 2 million fans are waiting. Each seat must be sold at most once, a fan has 10 minutes to pay after picking a seat, and unpaid seats go back on sale.

Today, every seat is a row in one PostgreSQL primary. The checkout service runs `SELECT ... WHERE status = 'free'` and then `UPDATE ... SET status = 'held'` in two separate statements. During the last big sale the database hit 100% CPU in the first 30 seconds, some seats were sold twice, and the payment provider double-charged fans whose browsers retried a timed-out request.

scenarios.title: Chat for a million rooms
scenarios.scenario:
A team chat product has 20 million daily active users and about 1 million active rooms. Clients hold a WebSocket to one of roughly 400 gateway servers behind a layer-4 load balancer. Messages must appear in the same order for everyone in a room, survive a gateway crash, and show up on a user's other devices.

Most rooms have fewer than 50 members. A few company-wide announcement rooms have 200,000 members. The current design writes each message to a database and then has the sending gateway loop over every member to push it.

scenarios.title: The metrics pipeline that fell behind
scenarios.scenario:
An observability vendor ingests metrics from customer agents. Each agent sends a batch every 10 seconds over HTTPS to stateless collectors, which publish to a Kafka topic with 64 partitions keyed by `customer_id`. Consumers aggregate the data into 1-minute rollups and write them to a columnar store.

After onboarding one very large customer, one partition's consumer lag grows without bound while the other 63 are nearly idle. Dashboards for that customer are now 40 minutes behind, and an on-call engineer proposes simply raising the partition count to 256.
